How many waves were there, and how many days did the longest one last?
The streaks of days above 30 last 3, 1, 4 and 2 days. Only two reach 3: there were
30 does not count: it has to be
than 30. That is why the seventh day breaks the streak.

outputs.text: how many waves there were and how many days the longest lasted.

relation.text: a wave is a streak of 3 or more days in a row above 30.

examples.text: the one in the task → 2 waves, the longest of 4.
the last three days above 30 → the wave ends with the data and it also counts.
a streak of exactly 3 days → it is a wave.

blocks.description: The same array of seven temperatures drawn six times. Walking visits them all; counting marks the ones that meet a condition and gives a number; accumulating gathers them all into a total; searching marks up to the first one that meets it and stops; filtering keeps the ones that meet it in another array; transforming changes each one and gives another array of the same length.

caption.text: Six patterns over the same collection. Almost every problem combines two or three.

runs.text: Days 1 to 4: the streak reaches 3 and breaks with the 29. It is the first wave.
Days 5 and 6: a 1-day streak; not a wave.
Day 7: the 30 breaks the streak, because it is not more than 30.
Days 8 to 11: a 4-day streak. It is the second wave, and the longest.
Days 13 and 14: a streak of 2 that ends with the data. It is checked after the loop: not a wave.
There is no new construction: you combine the ones you know. A follower can also remember just the previous value. For example, to count how many times a day was hotter than the one before:
